title: Tuckman & Belbin
blurb: Use Tuckman's five stages to read where a team is and lead it, and Belbin's nine roles to check it has the behaviours it needs.
question: An energy company's smart-meter rollout team has argued for weeks over methods, and a team role review shows three Plants, two Shapers and no Completer Finisher. Using Tuckman and Belbin, explain what is happening and what the project manager should do.

teach.body: TUCKMAN answers 'how does a team develop over time?' Teams pass through five stages: forming, storming, norming, performing and adjourning, and the leader's role changes at each. BELBIN answers 'what mix of behaviours does a team need?' He identified nine team roles in three groups: thinking, action and people. A project manager uses Tuckman to diagnose the team's stage and adapt their leadership, and Belbin to build a balanced team and spot missing behaviours.

steps.label: Forming
steps.sub: Polite, unsure of roles, dependent on the leader

steps.label: Storming
steps.sub: Members assert themselves; conflict over roles, methods and leader

steps.label: Norming
steps.sub: Ways of working agreed; cohesion and trust grow

steps.label: Performing
steps.sub: High performance, autonomy and mutual support

steps.label: Adjourning
steps.sub: Work complete; team disbands; pride and some loss

teach.caption: Teams can slip back: new members, a new leader or a big change in scope can return a performing team to storming.

teach.h: The leader's role at each stage
head: Stage
What the leader does
Style
rows: Sets purpose, objectives, roles and ground rules
Surfaces and resolves conflict; re-clarifies roles
Steps back, removes blockers, develops people
Recognises success, captures lessons, releases people
teach.caption: The style column links Tuckman to situational leadership: the more mature the team, the less direction it needs.

teach.h: Why a project manager uses Tuckman
teach.body: It tells you that storming is normal, so you manage the conflict rather than panic about it. It tells you how to lead now, and when to step back. It reminds you to plan time for forming and storming in the schedule, and to expect regression when membership changes. In a LINEAR project, specialists join by phase, so the team may re-form several times. In an ITERATIVE project, a stable team can reach performing and stay there, with retrospectives helping it norm quickly.

teach.h: Each role's strength and allowable weakness
head: Role
Contributes
Allowable weakness
rows: Inflexible; slow to see new options
teach.caption: An allowable weakness is the flip side of a strength. The PM tolerates it rather than trying to train it out.

teach.h: How a project manager uses Belbin, and its limits
teach.body: Team roles describe BEHAVIOUR, not job titles or authority. Most people have two or three preferred roles, so a small team can still cover all nine. The PM uses Belbin to check balance when selecting people, spot missing or doubled-up roles, allocate work to suit preferences and help people value each other's differences. Used rigidly, it labels people and boxes them in, so treat it as a conversation starter, not a verdict.

Week 6: the team is STORMING, with two Shapers clashing over the install method. The PM coaches: brings the disagreement into the open, agrees decision criteria and re-confirms who owns what. Belbin shows three Plants and no Completer Finisher, which explains the stream of new ideas and the sloppy install records. The PM pairs a detail-minded engineer with the records work and asks the Monitor Evaluator-leaning planner to test ideas before adoption.

teach.text: Storming is a NORMAL stage, not proof of a bad team: reject options that suppress, ignore or 'restructure away' the conflict. Never delegate fully during forming or storming. For Belbin, the groups are tested: Plant, Monitor Evaluator and Specialist are THINKING; Shaper, Implementer and Completer Finisher are ACTION; Co-ordinator, Teamworker and Resource Investigator are PEOPLE. The Co-ordinator is a people role even though it sounds like a manager.

teach.h: How this comes up in a written answer
items: Name the Tuckman stage from the symptoms and say it is a normal part of development.
State the leader's role at that stage (direct, coach, support, delegate, or recognise and release).
Explain that teams can regress after changes in membership or scope, and how the PM responds.
Use Belbin to identify missing or duplicated roles and the risk each creates.
Say what the PM will do: rebalance, pair or allocate work, treating roles as preferences, not labels.
Tuckman: forming, storming, norming, performing, adjourning; teams can slip back.
Leader's role: direct, coach, support, delegate, then recognise and release.
Belbin: nine roles; Thinking (Plant, Monitor Evaluator, Specialist), Action (Shaper, Implementer, Completer Finisher), People (Co-ordinator, Teamworker, Resource Investigator).
Every role has an allowable weakness; most people have two or three preferred roles.
Use both to diagnose and balance the team, not to label people.

summary: You can now name Tuckman's five stages in order, recognise each from a team's behaviour and say how the leader should act at each. You can also name Belbin's nine roles in their three groups and use them to spot gaps and imbalances in a project team.

A.q: Which is the correct order of Tuckman's stages of team development?
A.why: The order is forming, storming, norming, performing, adjourning: the team must work through conflict before it can agree norms and then perform.

whyNot.0: Norming comes after storming, not before it: norms are agreed once the conflict has been worked through.
whyNot.1: A team has to form before it can storm.
whyNot.3: Performing follows norming; a team can't perform well before it has agreed how to work.

A.q: To which Belbin group do the Co-ordinator, Teamworker and Resource Investigator belong?
A.why: These three are the people-oriented roles: they focus on goals, relationships and contacts.

whyNot.1: The thinking roles are Plant, Monitor Evaluator and Specialist.
whyNot.2: The action roles are Shaper, Implementer and Completer Finisher.
whyNot.3: Belbin has no 'leading' group; his three groups are thinking, action and people.

A.q: A project team that has worked closely for eighteen months is being disbanded at handover. Which leader action fits this stage best?
options: Set ground rules for the next phase
Delegate decisions to the strongest member
Introduce new challenge to raise output
A.why: In adjourning, the leader recognises the team's achievements, captures lessons learned and helps people move on to their next roles.

whyNot.0: Setting ground rules is a forming activity for a new team.
whyNot.1: Delegating to a strong member suits a performing team, not one being disbanded.
whyNot.2: The work is finished; adding challenge now misreads the stage.

B.q: After a heated fortnight of debate about the test approach, a team has agreed how to work and members now share work freely. What should the project manager do now?
options: Decide the approach for them now
Step back from all decisions fully
Re-run the kick-off to reset rules
B.why: The team has moved into norming. The leader's role is supporting: facilitating, sharing decision-making and building ownership.

whyNot.0: Imposing decisions is directing, which suits forming and would undo the ownership now growing.
whyNot.2: Stepping back entirely is delegating, which suits a performing team; norming teams still need support.
whyNot.3: The team has just agreed its ways of working; resetting them would push it backwards.

B.q: Which Belbin role has the allowable weakness of being inclined to worry unduly and reluctant to delegate?
B.why: The Completer Finisher's painstaking care over detail comes with a tendency to worry and to keep work rather than hand it over.

whyNot.1: The Implementer's allowable weakness is being somewhat inflexible and slow to respond to new possibilities.
whyNot.2: The Monitor Evaluator's allowable weakness is lacking drive and the ability to inspire others.
whyNot.3: The Specialist's allowable weakness is contributing only on a narrow front.

B.q: Which statement about Belbin's team roles is correct?
options: Each person has one fixed team role
A team needs nine people to cover all roles
Most people have two or three preferred roles
B.why: People usually have two or three preferred team roles (and some they can manage), which is why a small team can still cover all nine behaviours.

whyNot.0: Roles are behavioural preferences and people typically have more than one.
whyNot.1: Because people have several preferred roles, a team doesn't need nine members.
whyNot.2: Team roles describe how people behave in a team, not their job title or authority.

C.q: A digital agency's iterative team reached performing after four sprints. Two developers then leave and three join; stand-ups become tense and estimates are disputed. What is the BEST interpretation and response?
options: Performing: leave the team to settle
C.why: A change in membership has sent the team back to storming. The PM should recognise this as normal, coach the team through the conflict and re-clarify roles and ways of working.

whyNot.0: Regression after changes is normal, not failure; replacing people would cause yet more disruption.
whyNot.1: The project isn't ending, so this isn't adjourning.
whyNot.2: The tension shows the team is no longer performing; leaving it alone risks prolonged conflict.

C.q:
A team role review shows a team made up of Implementers, Completer Finishers and Specialists. The client brief needs fresh thinking and links with outside partners. Which TWO roles would best fill the gaps?
1) Plant
2) Monitor Evaluator
3) Resource Investigator
4) Teamworker
C.why: The Plant supplies original ideas and the Resource Investigator explores outside contacts and opportunities: exactly the two gaps described.

whyNot.0: A Monitor Evaluator judges ideas but doesn't generate them or build outside links.
whyNot.2: Neither the Monitor Evaluator nor the Teamworker brings fresh ideas or outside contacts.
whyNot.3: The Resource Investigator fits, but a Teamworker builds harmony rather than fresh thinking.

C.q: Two Shapers on a storming team keep clashing as each pushes their own approach. Which action uses Tuckman and Belbin together most effectively?
options: Remove one Shaper so the storm ends
Delegate fully, as Shapers like autonomy
Agree how each Shaper's drive is used
Ignore it, as storming resolves itself
C.why: Storming needs coaching and clear roles, and Belbin explains why two Shapers collide. Giving each a distinct area to drive keeps their energy while reducing the clash.

whyNot.0: Removing someone loses valuable drive and treats normal storming as a fault.
whyNot.1: Full delegation suits performing teams; during storming it leaves the conflict unmanaged.
whyNot.3: Unmanaged storming can drag on, damaging trust and delaying the work.

reteach.title: Think of it like a band making its first album
reteach.question: Picture five musicians forming a band to record an album. How do Tuckman's stages and Belbin's roles show up?

blocks.h: From strangers to a tight band
blocks.body: At first they're polite and wait for the producer to lead (forming). Then come the rows over musical direction (storming). They settle on a sound and a rehearsal routine (norming), and soon they're recording takes without being told (performing). When the album's done, they celebrate and go their separate ways (adjourning). Meanwhile the songwriter is the Plant, the manager booking gigs is the Resource Investigator, and the sound engineer fixing every last glitch is the Completer Finisher.

items.label: Forming
items.sub: Polite; the producer sets the plan

items.label: Storming
items.sub: Rows over the sound; producer coaches

blocks.text: A band of five songwriters writes great songs but never finishes the album. Balance of Belbin roles matters more than raw talent.

explain.body: Forming: polite, cautious, unclear roles, dependent on the leader. Storming: open disagreement over roles, methods and the leader. Norming: agreed ways of working and growing trust. Performing: high output and autonomy. Adjourning: work done, team disbands.

test.q: In a new team's meetings, members agree with every suggestion, then raise doubts privately with the PM afterwards. Which stage is this most likely?
test.why: Surface politeness with doubts kept private is typical of forming: people are cautious and avoid open conflict while they work out where they fit.

whyNot.0: In storming the disagreement comes out into the open.
whyNot.2: Norming teams have enough trust to discuss doubts openly in the meeting.
whyNot.3: Performing teams raise and tackle issues openly and quickly.

explain.body: Direct in forming (purpose, roles, ground rules). Coach in storming (bring conflict into the open, clarify roles). Support in norming (facilitate, share decisions). Delegate in performing (step back, remove blockers). In adjourning, recognise achievement, capture lessons and release people well.

test.q: Which leadership style best fits a team at the performing stage?
test.why: A performing team is capable and committed, so the leader delegates and focuses on removing blockers and developing people.

whyNot.0: Directing suits forming, when the team needs structure and clarity.
whyNot.1: Coaching suits storming, when the team needs help through conflict.
whyNot.2: Supporting suits norming, as the team builds ownership.

explain.body: Thinking: Plant, Monitor Evaluator, Specialist. Action: Shaper, Implementer, Completer Finisher. People: Co-ordinator, Teamworker, Resource Investigator. Each role brings a strength and an allowable weakness that comes with it.

test.q: Which Belbin group contains the Plant, Monitor Evaluator and Specialist?
test.why: The Plant, Monitor Evaluator and Specialist are Belbin's thinking (cerebral) roles.

whyNot.0: Action roles are Shaper, Implementer and Completer Finisher.
whyNot.1: People roles are Co-ordinator, Teamworker and Resource Investigator.

explain.body: Use it to check balance, spot missing or duplicated roles, allocate work to suit preferences and help people appreciate each other. Don't use it to grant authority, rank people or fix them in one box: roles are behavioural preferences that can flex with the situation.

test.q: Which is NOT an appropriate use of Belbin team roles by a project manager?
options: Spotting roles the team lacks or doubles
test.why: Belbin describes behavioural contributions. Formal authority comes from the project's governance and organisation structure, not from a team role.

whyNot.1: Matching work to people's preferred behaviours is a good use of Belbin.
whyNot.2: Checking for gaps and duplication is one of Belbin's main uses.
whyNot.3: Helping people appreciate different contributions reduces friction and is a sound use.
